column1: # Dataset: National Business Survivability Scores by City (2026)
# Description: City-level survivability rankings for 500+ business types across the US. Scores predict the projected chance a business type lasts 2+ years.
# Scores are based on 100+ location factors and 570

# Columns: city = Metro slug (24 metros).; business_subtype = Business type slug (110 types).; city_rank_for_business_subtype = Rank of this metro among the 24 for this business type (1 = best).; tier_of_city_for_business_subtype = Great
column4: from that rank.; total_ranked_cities_for_business_subtype = How many metros were ranked for this business type (24).; avg_survivability_score_for_business_subtype_in_city = The headline number: the projected chance
column6: that this business type lasts two or more years at a typical address in this metro. Use it to answer 'which city is best for X'.; the rest are in the README

column2: Which city is best for a given business? Filter business_subtype to the type
column3: sort by avg_survivability_score_for_business_subtype_in_city descending; city_rank_for_business_subtype is the same order as a number.

column2: How wide is the gap between the best and worst city? For one business_subtype
column3: subtract the lowest avg score from the highest. Gaps between cities are small (usually under 6 points); gaps between neighborhoods inside a city are far larger
column4: so use the metro file for the real decision.

column2: Where inside the best city should I look? Take the top city from this file
column3: open that metro's file (linked from source_article_url and the datasets page)
column4: and apply the first recipe there.
